questions.q: Why isn't informally eyeballing a handful of answers a sufficient way to evaluate a RAG pipeline?
options: It requires a graph database to run
It doesn't scale past a demo and can't isolate which part of the pipeline is actually underperforming
It only works for embedding models, not LLMs
It is slower than running the full test set through evaluate()
questions.explain: Tuning the trade-offs covered throughout this chapter requires measurement at scale, with metrics that pinpoint the specific failure rather than a vague overall impression.

options: Of the chunks that should have been retrieved, how many actually were
Of the chunks that were retrieved, how many were actually relevant
Whether the final answer addresses the question asked
Whether the final answer sticks to what the retrieved context says
questions.explain: Context recall measures whether retrieval found the truly relevant chunks that exist in the collection, not just how clean the chunks it did retrieve were.

questions.q: What does 'faithfulness' measure, as distinct from 'answer relevancy'?
options: Faithfulness measures retrieval speed; answer relevancy measures embedding cost
Faithfulness measures whether the generated answer sticks to what the retrieved context actually supports; answer relevancy measures whether the answer addresses the question asked
They measure the exact same thing under different names
Faithfulness only applies to citations; answer relevancy only applies to re-ranking
questions.explain: An answer can be faithful to its retrieved context while still wandering off-topic from the actual question — faithfulness and answer relevancy catch two different failure modes.

questions.q: In the Ragas evaluation example, what four fields does each test case need?
options: model, max_tokens, system, messages
chunk_size, chunk_overlap, separators, document_text
vector, limit, with_payload, score_threshold
user_input, retrieved_contexts, response, and reference
questions.explain: Each Ragas test case needs the question (user_input), what was actually retrieved (retrieved_contexts), what the pipeline actually answered (response), and a known-good answer to compare against (reference).

questions.q: Why should a trustworthy evaluation test set include questions the pipeline should honestly refuse to answer?
options: Because Ragas requires at least one failing test case to run
Because a test set built only from questions the pipeline already handles well will always report good scores, whether or not that reflects production behavior
Because abstention questions run faster than normal questions
Because context precision cannot be computed without them
questions.explain: Including cases where the honest answer is 'I don't know' lets the evaluation measure whether the pipeline abstains correctly, not just whether it performs well on easy, already-handled questions.
